rewritten_text:
When my tears stopped, reason and memory returned. I began to think more calmly about what had happened and what I ought to do. Only a few hours had passed, yet my life had changed completely. Since that morning, I seemed to have lived through years. My father was dead to me. For a moment I imagined him lying white-haired in his coffin, and myself, no longer young but nearing old age, mourning his death at its proper time. Yet that was not true. I was still young—oh, much too young! And to other people he was still alive. But I, in my misery, must never see him or speak to him again. I must flee him more urgently than I would my greatest enemy. Alone or among crowds, I must never look upon him again. This thought left me gasping with grief. It took such a hold on my mind that for a while I could think of nothing else. From now on, I decided, I would live in the bleakest isolation. I would go to the Continent and become a nun, not out of religious devotion, since I was not Catholic, but to shut myself away from the world forever. There I could weep alone, where the voices of the living would never reach me.

But my father—my beloved, desperately unhappy father? Would he die? Would he never conquer the violent passion that ruled him so mercilessly? Perhaps many, many years from now, when age had cooled the burning feelings tormenting him, he might become my father again. The thought eased my frown, and I felt a faint, sad smile soften the suffering on my lips. I wept to feel it. I dared to hope for a better future. Years would have to pass, but hope would make them fly. Even if they dragged painfully, they would still pass, and I would not have lost my father forever. Let him spend another sixteen years wandering in loneliness. Let him once again cry out his wild complaints to vast forests and mighty waterfalls in a foreign land. Let him face terrible dangers and hardships that break the spirit. Let the southern sun once more scorch his cheeks, worn by passion, and cold night rains fall on him and chill his blood.

To such a life I condemn you, miserable father! Go! Spend your days among savages and your nights beneath the open sky! Let your limbs wear out and your heart grow cold, until all youth within you is dead!

At least, that was what he thought. But how could he be sure? ... No. There had been nothing else behind it. Vanity had made him spare her. He had hypocritically pretended to be good. He had tried self-denial simply to satisfy his curiosity. He understood that now.

But would the murder haunt him for the rest of his life? Must his past always weigh upon him? Was he really going to confess? Never. Only one piece of evidence remained against him: the picture itself. That was the evidence. He would destroy it. Why had he kept it all this time? He had once enjoyed watching it change and grow old. Lately it had brought him no pleasure. It had stopped him sleeping. Whenever he went away, he had been terrified that someone else might see it. It had cast sadness over his passions. Just remembering it had spoiled countless happy moments. It had served as his conscience. Yes, it had been his conscience. He would destroy it.

Looking around, he saw the knife he had used to stab Basil Hallward. He had cleaned it over and over until no stain remained. It shone brightly. It had killed the painter; now it would kill the painter’s work and everything that work represented. It would kill the past. Once the past was dead, he would be free. It would end this monstrous life of his soul. Without its hideous warnings, he would find peace. He grabbed the knife and plunged it into the picture.

A scream rang out, followed by a crash. The scream was so full of terrible agony that the servants woke in fear and crept from their bedrooms. Two gentlemen walking through the square below stopped and looked up at the large house. They continued until they found a policeman, then brought him back. He rang the bell several times, but nobody answered. The house was dark apart from a light in an upper window. Eventually he withdrew to a nearby porch and stood watching.

“Who lives there, Constable?” asked the older gentleman.

“Mr. Dorian Gray, sir,” the policeman replied.

As the two men walked away, they exchanged scornful looks. One was Sir Henry Ashton’s uncle.

Inside the servants’ quarters, the partly dressed servants whispered among themselves. Old Mrs. Leaf cried and twisted her hands together. Francis was deathly pale.

After roughly fifteen minutes, he gathered the coachman and one of the footmen, and they crept upstairs.

Do not misunderstand me: I was never truly mad. Even when my wild thoughts seemed to be driving me insane, I knew what was happening to me. I revealed those thoughts only in silence and solitude. The people around me saw none of this. They saw only an unhappy girl whose spirit was broken, who spoke softly and gently, and whose lowered eyes sometimes shed tears that she tried to hide. They saw someone who preferred to be alone, avoided attention, and never smiled. No, I never smiled. That was all they knew.

Well, I escaped. I left my guardian’s home and was never heard from again. The letters I left, together with other circumstances I had carefully arranged, led people to believe that I had killed myself. As a result, they searched less thoroughly than they otherwise would have. Soon every trace and memory of me disappeared. I sailed from London in a small ship heading for a port in northern England. Now that my attempt had succeeded and I was completely alone, peace returned. The sea was calm, and the ship moved gently forward. I sat on deck beneath the open sky and felt like a different person. I was no longer the wild, frantic, deeply miserable Mathilda. I was a young woman committed to a hermit’s solitude, who must work to keep her heart free of turmoil and unholy despair. The unusual dress I had chosen, resembling a nun’s habit; the knowledge that only I knew I still existed; the loneliness in which I would spend the rest of my life—all these encouraged gentle thoughts in my wounded heart. The breeze moving through my hair revived me. Quietly I watched sunlight sparkling on the waves and birds chasing one another over the water, their feathers barely touching its surface. I slept without troubling dreams and woke refreshed, ready to enjoy my peaceful freedom again.

Four days later we reached our destination. I did not want to stay near the coast, so I went inland at once. I had already decided what sort of place I would live in: an isolated house on a broad plain, far from any other home. There I could see the entire horizon and walk for miles without being disturbed by the sight of another person. I did not hate humanity, but I felt that my emotions could remain gentle only if I lived alone. I settled in a wide, lonely place, on a bleak heath scattered with stones. Short grass grew between them, and here and there a few rushes stood beside a small pool.
